Table 11 describes the major equipment applied in the DAC plant along with their respective types and design conditions. The adsorption blower and cooling air blower 40 have inlet conditions as specified in the previous section, while outlet conditions and driver power are influenced by pressure drops predicted using Aspen Adsorption. These blowers may subsequently be subdivided into multiple units, depending on commercial availability and vendor- sizing constraints. A primary condenser located upstream of the vacuum pump removes a significant fraction of the desorbed water, as reflected in the stream data presented in Table 12. To prevent water accumulation within the pump, interstage water cooling was implemented to maintain the process stream at approximately 60°C. A secondary condenser downstream of the pump removes the remaining water fraction prior to the multistage reciprocating compressor, whose power demand is determined by the required product delivery pressure. Stream properties throughout the process were evaluated using Aspen Plus. The stream properties in Table 12, based on the process layout shown in Figure 40, illustrate the key transformations of the flow across each major equipment unit, as well as the characteristics of both the vent and product streams in the DAC plant. These data provide the basis for evaluating process performance, identifying mass transfer requirements, and supporting subsequent equipment sizing and cost estimation. Table 12. Water and energy balances The water balance for the DAC plant is given in Table 13. As shown, the majority of the water demand is associated with Condenser 1, which is responsible for separating the bulk of the desorbed water. However, the system also generates water as a byproduct, which can be recovered and reused as makeup for the plant’s equipment.
